records.title: CD38 is critical for social behaviour by regulating oxytocin secretion
records.authors: Duo Jin; Hong-Xiang Liu; Hirokazu Hirai; Takashi Torashima; Taku Nagai; Olga Lopatina; Natalia A. Shnayder; Kiyofumi Yamada; Mami Noda; Toshihiro Seike; Kyota Fujita; Shin Takasawa; Shigeru Yokoyama; Keita Koizumi; Yoshitake Shiraishi; Shigenori Tanaka; Minako Hashii; Toru Yoshihara; Kazuhiro Higashida; Mohammad Saharul Islam; Nobuaki Yamada; Kenshi Hayashi; Naoya Noguchi; Ichiro Kato; Hiroshi Okamoto; Akihiro Matsushima; Alla Salmina; Toshio Munesue; Nobuaki Shimizu; Sumiko Mochida; Masahide Asano; Haruhiro Higashida
records.finding: Mice lacking CD38 had reduced oxytocin secretion and impaired maternal and social behaviour. Oxytocin administration or restoration of CD38 rescued aspects of the behavioural changes, linking CD38-dependent calcium signalling to oxytocin release.
records.limitation: A mechanistic animal study; it does not establish a clinical treatment effect in humans.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Oxytocin secretion, calcium signalling and social behaviour
evidence.relationshipNote: A mechanistic animal study; it does not establish a clinical treatment effect in humans.

records.title: Social reward requires coordinated activity of nucleus accumbens oxytocin and serotonin
records.authors: Gül Dölen; Ayeh Darvishzadeh; Kee Wui Huang; Robert C. Malenka
records.finding: In mice, social reward required coordinated oxytocin and serotonin signalling in the nucleus accumbens. Removing oxytocin receptors from dorsal raphe inputs, or blocking accumbens serotonin 5-HT1B receptors, prevented the rewarding effect of social interaction.
records.limitation: The experiments identify a mouse neural mechanism. They do not measure SLC6A4 gene expression or test a human therapy.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Receptor deletion, pharmacology, synaptic responses and social reward
evidence.relationshipNote: The experiments identify a mouse neural mechanism. They do not measure SLC6A4 gene expression or test a human therapy.

records.title: Evidence for the existence of dopamine d2-oxytocin receptor heteromers in the ventral and dorsal striatum with facilitatory receptor–receptor interactions
records.authors: W Romero-Fernandez; D O Borroto-Escuela; L F Agnati; K Fuxe
records.finding: The authors report dopamine D2–oxytocin receptor complexes in the ventral and dorsal striatum, with facilitatory interactions between the receptors. The findings provide a molecular explanation to investigate alongside wider evidence linking dopamine and oxytocin to social behaviour.
records.limitation: Receptor interactions in laboratory preparations do not establish their clinical importance or demonstrate a change in gene expression.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Laboratory receptor-interaction study; research letter. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.sample: Laboratory receptor and rat striatal preparations
evidence.measurement: Receptor proximity and functional receptor interactions
evidence.relationshipNote: Receptor interactions in laboratory preparations do not establish their clinical importance or demonstrate a change in gene expression.

records.title: The neural mechanisms and circuitry of the pair bond
records.authors: Hasse Walum; Larry J. Young
records.finding: This review describes how oxytocin, dopamine and vasopressin interact with reward and social-memory circuits during pair-bond formation and maintenance. It connects experimental work in prairie voles and other animals with questions about human attachment.
records.limitation: A narrative synthesis with substantial animal evidence; it is not a pooled estimate of a human treatment effect.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Narrative review. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.sample: Animal studies and human attachment research
evidence.measurement: Review of neural circuits and receptor mechanisms
evidence.relationshipNote: A narrative synthesis with substantial animal evidence; it is not a pooled estimate of a human treatment effect.

records.title: Quantitative cellular-resolution map of the oxytocin receptor in postnatally developing mouse brains
records.authors: Kyra T. Newmaster; Zachary T. Nolan; Uree Chon; Daniel J. Vanselow; Abigael R. Weit; Manal Tabbaa; Shizu Hidema; Katsuhiko Nishimori; Elizabeth A. D. Hammock; Yongsoo Kim
records.finding: Cellular-resolution maps show that oxytocin receptor expression changes across brain regions and postnatal development in mice. Reporter imaging and RNA measurements identify transient cortical expression and region-specific patterns, providing an anatomical reference for oxytocin research.
records.limitation: Mouse developmental maps do not establish the corresponding receptor distribution or functional connections in the human brain.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental developmental brain-mapping study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Oxytocin receptor reporter imaging and in situ RNA measurements
evidence.relationshipNote: Mouse developmental maps do not establish the corresponding receptor distribution or functional connections in the human brain.

records.title: Oxytocin mediates early experience–dependent cross-modal plasticity in the sensory cortices
records.authors: Jing-Jing Zheng; Shu-Jing Li; Xiao-Di Zhang; Wan-Ying Miao; Dinghong Zhang; Haishan Yao; Xiang Yu
records.finding: Early sensory deprivation altered oxytocin synthesis and release and reduced excitatory synaptic transmission across sensory cortices in mice. Oxytocin treatment restored aspects of this transmission, linking early sensory experience to oxytocin-dependent cortical plasticity.
records.limitation: Experiments in developing mice; the study does not test EMDR, music therapy or a human clinical intervention.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.sample: Developing mice exposed to sensory deprivation
evidence.measurement: Oxytocin synthesis and release; cortical synaptic transmission
evidence.relationshipNote: Experiments in developing mice; the study does not test EMDR, music therapy or a human clinical intervention.

records.title: Oxytocin-dependent reopening of a social reward learning critical period with MDMA
records.authors: Romain Nardou; Eastman M. Lewis; Rebecca Rothhaas; Ran Xu; Aimei Yang; Edward Boyden; Gül Dölen
records.finding: In adult mice, MDMA reopened a developmental period for social-reward learning. The effect involved oxytocin-dependent plasticity in the nucleus accumbens, connecting serotonergic drug action with oxytocin signalling and social learning.
records.limitation: An animal mechanism study. SLC6A4 is indexed for serotonin-transporter involvement, not a measured change in its gene expression. The study does not establish human treatment efficacy.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Social-reward learning, pharmacology and synaptic plasticity
evidence.relationshipNote: An animal mechanism study. SLC6A4 is indexed for serotonin-transporter involvement, not a measured change in its gene expression. The study does not establish human treatment efficacy.

records.title: Functional involvement of septal miR-132 in extinction and oxytocin-mediated reversal of social fear
records.authors: Anna Bludau; Uwe Schwartz; Daniela M. Zeitler; Melanie Royer; Gunter Meister; Inga D. Neumann; Rohit Menon
records.finding: Septal miR-132 contributed to social-fear extinction and oxytocin-mediated reversal of social fear in male mice. Manipulation in oxytocin-receptor-expressing neurons linked this microRNA to behavioural responses and downstream Gdf5 regulation.
records.limitation: The molecular and behavioural findings come from male mice; they do not establish a therapy or biomarker for human social anxiety.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse molecular study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Septal microRNA expression and manipulation; social-fear behaviour
evidence.relationshipNote: The molecular and behavioural findings come from male mice; they do not establish a therapy or biomarker for human social anxiety.

records.title: Effects of intranasal oxytocin on fear extinction learning
records.authors: Mahmoud Rashidi; Joe J. Simon; Katja Bertsch; Gerhard Vincent Wegen; Beate Ditzen; Herta Flor; Valery Grinevich; Robert Christian Wolf; Sabine C. Herpertz
records.finding: In 124 healthy women, intranasal oxytocin impaired fear-extinction learning relative to placebo. The result challenges the assumption that oxytocin uniformly improves extinction and highlights the importance of timing and experimental context.
records.limitation: Healthy participants completed a laboratory conditioning task. The trial did not test a clinical PTSD treatment or measure gene expression.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: The article reports a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human experiment. Its outcome is laboratory fear extinction.

evidence.measurement: Fear conditioning and extinction responses
evidence.relationshipNote: Healthy participants completed a laboratory conditioning task. The trial did not test a clinical PTSD treatment or measure gene expression.

records.title: Interdependency between oxytocin and dopamine in trust-based learning in mice
records.authors: Samuel Budniok; Zsuzsanna Callaerts-Vegh; Marian Bakermans-Kranenburg; Guy Bosmans; Rudi D’Hooge
records.finding: Oxytocin and dopamine interacted during socially acquired food-preference learning in mice. Oxytocin affected updating after an aversive outcome, and dopamine depletion removed this effect, indicating dependence on intact dopaminergic signalling.
records.limitation: “Trust” is operationalised through a mouse food-learning task. The experiment does not directly measure human trust or DRD2 gene expression.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Social transmission of food preference and pharmacological manipulation
evidence.relationshipNote: “Trust” is operationalised through a mouse food-learning task. The experiment does not directly measure human trust or DRD2 gene expression.

records.title: Neural circuitry for maternal oxytocin release induced by infant cries
records.authors: Silvana Valtcheva; Habon A. Issa; Chloe J. Bair-Marshall; Kathleen A. Martin; Kanghoon Jung; Yiyao Zhang; Hyung-Bae Kwon; Robert C. Froemke
records.finding: Pup calls activated a thalamus-to-hypothalamus pathway that promoted maternal oxytocin release in mice. Prolonged disinhibition of oxytocin neurons linked an auditory social cue to neuropeptide release.
records.limitation: The study examines maternal responses to infant calls in mice. It does not test music, brain entrainment or human stress reduction.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse neural-circuit study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Neural recordings, circuit manipulation and oxytocin release
evidence.relationshipNote: The study examines maternal responses to infant calls in mice. It does not test music, brain entrainment or human stress reduction.

records.title: Epigenetic regulation of the glucocorticoid receptor in human brain associates with childhood abuse
records.authors: Patrick O McGowan; Aya Sasaki; Ana C D'Alessio; Sergiy Dymov; Benoit Labonté; Moshe Szyf; Gustavo Turecki; Michael J Meaney
records.design: Human postmortem observational study and laboratory assays
records.finding: Hippocampal tissue from suicide victims with a history of childhood abuse showed altered glucocorticoid-receptor promoter methylation and lower receptor transcript levels. Laboratory promoter assays supported a potential regulatory link between methylation and transcription.
records.limitation: Postmortem associations cannot establish that childhood adversity caused the molecular differences or that the pattern applies to every exposed person.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Human postmortem observational study and laboratory assays. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: NR3C1 promoter methylation and messenger RNA
evidence.relationshipNote: Postmortem associations cannot establish that childhood adversity caused the molecular differences or that the pattern applies to every exposed person.

records.title: Social stress induces neurovascular pathology promoting depression
records.authors: Caroline Menard; Madeline L. Pfau; Georgia E. Hodes; Veronika Kana; Victoria X. Wang; Sylvain Bouchard; Aki Takahashi; Meghan E. Flanigan; Hossein Aleyasin; Katherine B. LeClair; William G. Janssen; Benoit Labonté; Eric M. Parise; Zachary S. Lorsch; Sam A. Golden; Mitra Heshmati; Carol Tamminga; Gustavo Turecki; Matthew Campbell; Zahi A. Fayad; Cheuk Ying Tang; Miriam Merad; Scott J. Russo
records.design: Experimental mouse study with human postmortem comparison
records.finding: Chronic social stress reduced the tight-junction protein claudin-5 in susceptible mice, increasing blood–brain barrier permeability and allowing peripheral IL-6 into the brain. Reduced CLDN5 was also observed in postmortem tissue from people with depression.
records.limitation: Causal manipulations were performed in mice. IL-6 infiltration is a protein-level finding; the human comparison is observational.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse study with human postmortem comparison. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Blood–brain barrier permeability, CLDN5 expression and IL-6 protein
evidence.relationshipNote: Causal manipulations were performed in mice. IL-6 infiltration is a protein-level finding; the human comparison is observational.

records.title: NMDA receptor trafficking in synaptic plasticity and neuropsychiatric disorders
records.authors: C. Geoffrey Lau; R. Suzanne Zukin
records.finding: This review explains how NMDA receptor trafficking and subunit composition influence synaptic plasticity, and discusses their relevance to neuropsychiatric disorders. It provides background for interpreting activity-dependent changes in excitatory signalling.
records.limitation: NMDA denotes a receptor family. This review does not establish a direct OXTR interaction or the efficacy of a particular intervention.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Narrative review. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Review of receptor trafficking and synaptic plasticity
evidence.relationshipNote: NMDA denotes a receptor family. This review does not establish a direct OXTR interaction or the efficacy of a particular intervention.

records.title: The effect of music performance on the transcriptome of professional musicians
records.authors: Chakravarthi Kanduri; Tuire Kuusi; Minna Ahvenainen; Anju K. Philips; Harri Lähdesmäki; Irma Järvelä
records.finding: Whole-blood gene expression changed after a two-hour concert performed by professional musicians. Genes including SNCA, FOS and DUSP1 contributed to the reported response, with enrichment of pathways related to neuronal activity and plasticity.
records.limitation: Ten performers were compared with ten music-free controls. Blood transcription does not directly measure gene expression in the brain, and allocation was not randomized.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Controlled, non-randomized transcriptome study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Whole-blood transcriptome before and after two hours
evidence.relationshipNote: Ten performers were compared with ten music-free controls. Blood transcription does not directly measure gene expression in the brain, and allocation was not randomized.

records.title: Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music
records.authors: Valorie N Salimpoor; Mitchel Benovoy; Kevin Larcher; Alain Dagher; Robert J Zatorre
records.design: Human PET and functional MRI study
records.finding: Pleasurable music was associated with dopamine release in the striatum. Anticipation and peak emotional experience recruited different regions, with caudate involvement during anticipation and nucleus accumbens involvement during peak pleasure.
records.limitation: A small laboratory study of selected listeners. Dopamine release is not a measurement of DRD2 gene expression or a music-therapy outcome.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Human PET and functional MRI study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.sample: Healthy listeners selected for strong emotional responses to music
evidence.measurement: PET dopamine-sensitive radioligand imaging and fMRI
evidence.relationshipNote: A small laboratory study of selected listeners. Dopamine release is not a measurement of DRD2 gene expression or a music-therapy outcome.

records.title: Biological principles for music and mental health
records.authors: Daniel L. Bowling
records.finding: The authors organise music and mental-health research around biological principles involving reward, rhythm, learning and social connection. The review examines neural and physiological mechanisms, including dopamine and oxytocin signalling, that may help explain responses to music.
records.limitation: A broad mechanistic review; it does not supply one pooled treatment effect or establish that every music intervention acts through the same pathways.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Narrative review. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Review of biological mechanisms relevant to music and mental health
evidence.relationshipNote: A broad mechanistic review; it does not supply one pooled treatment effect or establish that every music intervention acts through the same pathways.

records.title: Brain correlates of music-evoked emotions
records.authors: Stefan Koelsch
records.finding: Neuroimaging research links music-evoked emotions to networks involving reward, autonomic regulation and emotional processing, including the nucleus accumbens, amygdala and hypothalamus. The review examines how musical structure and expectation engage these systems.
records.limitation: A review of mechanisms and brain responses; it does not estimate clinical efficacy for a defined music-therapy programme.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Narrative review. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Review of music-evoked emotion and brain activity
evidence.relationshipNote: A review of mechanisms and brain responses; it does not estimate clinical efficacy for a defined music-therapy programme.

records.title: Self-administered mindfulness interventions reduce stress in a large, randomized controlled multi-site study
records.authors: Alessandro Sparacio; Hans IJzerman; Ivan Ropovik; Filippo Giorgini; Christoph Spiessens; Bert N. Uchino; Joshua Landvatter; Tracey Tacana; Sandra J. Diller; Jaye L. Derrick; Joahana Segundo; Jace D. Pierce; Robert M. Ross; Zoë Francis; Amanda LaBoucane; Christine Ma-Kellams; Maire B. Ford; Kathleen Schmidt; Celia C. Wong; Wendy C. Higgins; Bryant M. Stone; Samantha K. Stanley; Gianni Ribeiro; Paul T. Fuglestad; Valerie Jaklin; Andrea Kübler; Philipp Ziebell; Crystal L. Jewell; Yulia Kovas; Mahnoosh Allahghadri; Charlotte Fransham; Michael F. Baranski; Hannah Burgess; Annika B. E. Benz; Maysa DeSousa; Catherine E. Nylin; Janae C. Brooks; Caitlyn M. Goldsmith; Jessica M. Benson; Siobhán M. Griffin; Stephen Dunne; William E. Davis; Tam J. Watermeyer; William B. Meese; Jennifer L. Howell; Laurel Standiford Reyes; Megan G. Strickland; Sally S. Dickerson; Samantha Pescatore; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Zachary I. Wunder; Martin V. Day; Shawna Brenton; Audrey H. Linden; Christopher E. Hawk; Léan V. O’Brien; Tenzin Urgyen; Jennifer S. McDonald; Kim Lien van der Schans; Heidi Blocker; Caroline Ng Tseung-Wong; Gabriela M. Jiga-Boy
records.finding: Across 37 sites and 2,239 participants, four brief self-administered mindfulness exercises reduced immediate self-reported stress compared with an active control. The body-scan exercise produced the largest reduction among the tested exercises.
records.limitation: The outcomes were short term and self-reported, with predominantly English-speaking participants in higher-income settings. Gene expression was not measured.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Random assignment and an active comparison are reported. A single- or double-blind classification is not established from the reviewed methods.

evidence.measurement: Immediate self-reported stress
evidence.relationshipNote: The outcomes were short term and self-reported, with predominantly English-speaking participants in higher-income settings. Gene expression was not measured.

records.title: Meditation and vacation effects have an impact on disease-associated molecular phenotypes
records.authors: E S Epel; E Puterman; J Lin; E H Blackburn; P Y Lum; N D Beckmann; J Zhu; E Lee; A Gilbert; R A Rissman; R E Tanzi; E E Schadt
records.design: Randomized retreat comparison with an observational experienced-meditator group
records.finding: A six-day resort stay was associated with substantial blood gene-expression changes in both meditation and vacation groups. Experienced meditators showed additional molecular patterns, but the randomized novice-meditation comparison did not establish a gene-expression advantage over vacation.
records.limitation: The experienced-meditator group was not randomized. Shared changes across groups cannot be attributed specifically to meditation.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Novices were randomized to meditation or vacation; experienced meditators formed a separate observational group. Masked molecular superiority of meditation was not established.

evidence.sample: Healthy women: meditation-naive participants randomized to retreat or vacation, plus experienced meditators
evidence.measurement: Blood transcriptome and disease-associated molecular phenotypes
evidence.relationshipNote: The experienced-meditator group was not randomized. Shared changes across groups cannot be attributed specifically to meditation.

records.title: Preliminary indications of the effect of a brief yoga intervention on markers of inflammation and DNA methylation in chronically stressed women
records.authors: K N Harkess; J Ryan; P H Delfabbro; S Cohen-Woods
records.design: Exploratory molecular substudy of a yoga trial
records.finding: An exploratory substudy in chronically stressed women reported lower methylation in a TNF region following a brief yoga intervention. Comparable regional changes were not found for IL6 or CRP, and a reduction in circulating inflammatory markers was not established.
records.limitation: The molecular sample contained 28 women. Its retrospective and uncontrolled longitudinal components limit causal interpretation, despite recruitment from a larger randomized trial.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Exploratory molecular substudy of a yoga trial. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.sample: 28 chronically stressed women from a larger trial
evidence.measurement: Targeted DNA methylation and inflammatory proteins
evidence.relationshipNote: The molecular sample contained 28 women. Its retrospective and uncontrolled longitudinal components limit causal interpretation, despite recruitment from a larger randomized trial.

records.title: Neural circuits underlying a psychotherapeutic regimen for fear disorders
records.authors: Jinhee Baek; Sukchan Lee; Taesup Cho; Seong-Wook Kim; Minsoo Kim; Yongwoo Yoon; Ko Keun Kim; Junweon Byun; Sang Jeong Kim; Jaeseung Jeong; Hee-Sup Shin
records.finding: Alternating bilateral visual stimulation during fear extinction recruited a superior-colliculus–thalamus–amygdala circuit in mice and reduced the return of conditioned fear. The experiments identify a possible neural mechanism relevant to eye-movement-based approaches.
records.limitation: A mouse model inspired by a psychotherapeutic component; it is not a trial of clinical EMDR or a self-administered treatment in humans.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Experimental mouse neural-circuit study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.measurement: Circuit manipulation, neural activity and conditioned fear
evidence.relationshipNote: A mouse model inspired by a psychotherapeutic component; it is not a trial of clinical EMDR or a self-administered treatment in humans.

records.title: Possible neural mechanisms of psychotherapy for trauma-related symptoms: cerebral responses to the neuropsychological treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder model individuals
records.authors: Tamaki Amano; Motomi Toichi
records.finding: During an EMDR-related procedure, healthy volunteers recalled moderately unpleasant memories while researchers measured cortical haemodynamic responses. The study examined temporal and orbitofrontal activity as possible correlates of memory processing.
records.limitation: Participants were model volunteers, not a clinical PTSD cohort. The study does not establish treatment efficacy or a gene-expression effect.

studyDesignAssessment.basis: Human experimental neuroimaging study. No masked human randomized trial classification is assigned.

evidence.sample: Healthy volunteers recalling moderately unpleasant memories
evidence.measurement: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy and subjective responses
evidence.relationshipNote: Participants were model volunteers, not a clinical PTSD cohort. The study does not establish treatment efficacy or a gene-expression effect.
